Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 59, verses 1–2:

Madaniyyah (revealed at Madinah). It has twenty-four verses [revealed after Surat al-Bayyinah].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The Banu al-Nadir made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they would be neither against him nor with him. When he prevailed at the Battle of Badr, they said: "He is the Prophet whose description is in the Torah; his banner will never be turned back." But when the Muslims were defeated at the Battle of Uhud, they had doubts and broke the treaty. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf went out with forty riders to Makkah, and they formed an alliance with the Quraysh at the Ka'bah. The Prophet (ﷺ) then ordered Muhammad ibn Maslamah al-Ansari, who killed Ka'b by treachery and was his foster-brother, to do so. Then he attacked them at dawn with troops, riding a donkey with a halter of palm fiber, and said to them: "Leave the city." They replied: "Death is more beloved to us than that." So they called to war [[I have not found a chain of narration for this; al-Tha'labi mentioned it in this form without a chain.]].

It is also said that they asked the Messenger of Allah for a delay of ten days to prepare for departure. Then Abdullah ibn Ubayy the hypocrite and his companions sent to them: "Do not leave your fortress. If they fight you, we are with you and will not abandon you; and if you go out, we will certainly go out with you." So they fortified the alleys and secured them [[His words "fa-darabu ala al-azqah" mean they narrowed their entrances with wood and stones, as can be understood from what follows about their destroying their houses with their own hands. In al-Sihah, "al-darb" (a dictionary by al-Jawhari) is a narrow passage in the mountain. (ʿAyn)]]. He besieged them for twenty-one nights. When Allah cast terror into their hearts and they despaired of the help of the hypocrites, they asked for peace. He refused them except on condition of exile, on the basis that each three households would load one camel with whatever belongings they wished. So they went into exile to Syria, to Jericho and Adhri'at, except for two households: the family of Abu al-Huqayq and the family of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who joined Khaybar. A group also joined al-Hirah.

The lam in ﴿li-awwali al-hashr﴾ ("at the first gathering") is connected to "akhraja" (He brought forth), like the lam in Allah's words ﴿Yā laytanī qaddamtu li-ḥayātī﴾ ("Oh, would that I had sent forth for my life," 89:24). [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The lam in His words ﴿li-awwali al-hashr﴾ is like the lam in His words ﴿qaddamtu li-ḥayātī﴾." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "It seems he means that it is the lam that accompanies a date, as in his saying: 'I wrote for such a year and for such a month,' and your saying: 'I came to him at such a time.']] The meaning is: "He brought out those who disbelieved at the first gathering." The meaning of "the first gathering" is that this was the first of their gatherings toward Syria. They were from a tribe that had never before been exiled, and they were the first of the People of the Book to be expelled from the Arabian Peninsula to Syria. Or it means: this was the first of their gatherings, and their last gathering was their expulsion from Khaybar to Syria by ʿUmar.

It is also said: their last gathering is the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, because the place of assembly will be in Syria. It is reported from ʿIkrimah: "Whoever doubts that the place of assembly is here, meaning Syria, let him recite this verse."

It is also said: the meaning is that He brought them out from their homes at the first gathering for fighting against them, because it was the first fight that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fought against them. ﴿You did not think that they would go out﴾, because of the strength of their might, the firmness of their defenses, the abundance of their numbers and their equipment, and because they thought their fortresses would protect them from the might of Allah. ﴿But the decree of Allah came upon them from where they did not expect﴾, from where they had not thought and it had not occurred to them: namely the killing of their chief Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf by surprise at the hand of his brother. That weakened their strength and diminished their power, and stripped their hearts of security and calm through the terror cast into them. He inspired them to cooperate with the believers in destroying their own homes and to help bring about their own ruin, and He discouraged the hypocrites who had been supporting them from aiding them. None of this had been in their calculations, and from it came their destruction.

If you say: what is the difference between your saying "and they thought their fortresses would prevent them" and "what protected them," and between the arrangement in which it came? I say: placing the predicate before the subject shows their extreme confidence in the strength of the fortresses and their protection of them, and making their pronoun the subject of "inna" and attributing the sentence to it shows their belief in themselves that they were in might and protection, so that they did not care about anyone who approached them or hoped to overpower them [[His words "aw yaṭmaʿu fi maʿāzzatihim" mean "or hoped to overpower them," as in al-Sihah.]]. That is not present in your saying "and they thought their fortresses would prevent them."

It is read ﴿fa-ma'atāhum Allāh﴾ ("so Allah came to them"), meaning: "so destruction came to them."

Al-ruʿb (terror) is fear that strikes the chest, that is, fills it. Qadhf (casting) means establishing and fixing it. From this they say of the lion: "muqadhdhaf" (cast), as if it were thrown with flesh thrown in a way that is not the same as its parts being loose and interlocked.

It is read ﴿yukharribūna﴾ and ﴿yukhribūna﴾, with the doubled and single letter. Al-takhrīb and al-ikhrāb mean corruption through breaking down and demolition. Al-kharibah (ruin) means corruption. They were destroying its interiors, and the Muslims its exteriors, because of what Allah willed of uprooting their foundations, and so that no house would remain for them in Madinah and no dwelling for them among them. What led them to destruction was their need for wood and stones to block the entrances of the alleys [[His words "min istiʾṣāl shaʾfatihim" (the uprooting of their root) refer to al-Sihah, where "al-shaʾfah" is a sore that comes out at the bottom of the foot and is cauterized and disappears; it is said in the proverb: "May Allah uproot its root," meaning: Allah removed it as that sore is removed by cauterization. (ʿAyn)]]. Also, after their exile, they would not regret leaving behind dwellings for the Muslims, and they would carry with them whatever was in their buildings of wood and fine teak. As for the believers, their motive was to remove their fortifications and defenses, and to widen the field of battle for them. If you say: what is the meaning of their destroying it with the hands of the believers? I say: since they exposed them to that and were the cause of it, it is as if they ordered them to do it and assigned it to them. ﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾ from what Allah arranged and facilitated regarding their expulsion and the empowerment of the Muslims over them without fighting.

It is also said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) promised the Muslims that Allah would give them their land and wealth as inheritance without fighting, and it happened as he said.

Min līnatin (of palm trees) is an explanation of "what you cut down." The position of mā is accusative, governed by qata'tum, as if he had said: "Whatever you cut down." The pronoun referring back to mā in His words "or you left them standing" is feminine (taraktumūhā) because it is in the sense of al-līna. Al-līna means the palm tree among the varieties of palms other than al-ʿajwa [[Al-Zamakhshari mentions two explanations of it, one of which is that it is the palms other than al-ʿajwa and al-barnī, the two best kinds of palm... etc. Aḥmad said:

It is apparent that the permission is general to both cutting and leaving, because it is the answer to a conditional clause implied by both, and the justification by the disgracing of the wicked applies to both. Cutting them down grieves them over their loss, and leaving them standing grieves them over their remaining for the Muslims to benefit from. Thus they are in two griefs from both matters together.]], and al-barniyya, which are the finest kinds of palms. Its yāʾ is substituted for a wāw, changed because of the kasra before it, like al-dīma. It is also said that al-līna is the noble palm tree, as if they derived it from al-līn (softness).

Dhū al-Rumma said: "As if my saddle-frame above her were a bird's nest, upon a līna, tall-stemmed, whose flanks sway."

[[Dhū al-Rumma describes his camel: al-qatūd are the wooden frames of the saddle without its fittings, made from al-qatād, a hard thorny tree.

Al-līna: the palm tree. Al-saw'āʾ: long-stemmed. Hafā al-rīḥ and al-baṣīr yahfū: ran swiftly. Al-janūb: a kind of wind. The pronoun in "her flanks" refers to the līna. He likens the wooden frames of the saddle above the camel to a bird's nest above a palm tree, and this entails likening the camel to the palm tree in height and nobility, which is the intended meaning. Were it said that using the first comparison for the second is metaphor, or that intending the second through the first is metonymy, it would not be far-fetched. In this there is an indication of likening her to the bird in caution and alertness. In his words "whose flanks sway" is an indication of the camel's swift pace and her cutting through the winds, like the swift passage of the wind over the palm tree; she cuts through it, as if she were moving through it swiftly.]]

Its plural is līn. It was read qawwamā, in its original form. There are two views on this: that it is a plural of the original form, like rahn and ruhun; or that the ḍamma sufficed in place of the wāw. It was also read qāiman, following its roots, going back to the wording of mā.

"So by Allah's permission": so cutting them was by Allah's permission and command. "And so that He might disgrace the wicked": and to humiliate the Jews and enrage them, permission was given to cut them. This is because when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded that their palms be cut down and burned, they said: "O Muhammad, you used to forbid corruption on the earth, so what is the matter with cutting down and burning the palms?" So there was something in the hearts of the believers because of that. Then it was revealed, meaning: Allah permitted them to cut them down so that He might increase your rage and double your grief when you see them disposing of your property as they wish and managing it as they please.[[Ibn Isḥāq related it in al-Maghāzī, and al-Ṭabarī from his route: "Yazīd ibn Rūmān narrated to us" and so on. Ibn Hishām mentioned it from Ibn Isḥāq without mentioning his shaykh. Ibn Mardawayh related it through Ibn Isḥāq from al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Al-Wāqidī mentioned in al-Maghāzī "that the one who was sent to the Prophet ﷺ was Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab." Abū Dāwūd related in al-Marāsīl through the route of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm something similar, abridged.]]

The scholars agreed that the fortresses and dwellings of the unbelievers may be demolished, burned, flooded, and bombarded with catapults, and likewise their trees, whether fruit-bearing or not, may be uprooted. It is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd: "They cut from them what was a place of fighting." If you say: why was al-līna singled out for cutting? I say: if it is of the varieties, then they should keep for themselves the ʿajwa and the barniyya; and if it is of the noble palms, then the rage of the Jews will be greater and more severe.

It is related that two men were cutting: one of them was cutting the ʿajwa and the other the līn. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked them, and this one said: "I left it for the Messenger of Allah," and that one said: "I cut it to enrage the unbelievers."[[I have not found it in this wording, but al-Bukhārī has it in al-Wāqidī: he appointed two of his companions over cutting and burning the palms: Abū Layla al-Māzinī and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām. Abū Layla would cut the ʿajwa and the other would cut the līn. They were asked about that. Abū Layla said: "The ʿajwa was more burning for them." Ibn Salām said: "It is known that Allah will grant them their property as spoils, and the ʿajwa was the best of their property," so Allah revealed the verse. Al-Bayhaqī related in al-Dalāʾil through the route of Ibn Abī Najīḥ from Mujāhid who said: "Some of the Muhajirun forbade others from cutting the palms, and said: 'It is only among the spoils of the Muslims.' Those who cut said: 'Rather it is a rage to the enemy.' Then the Qur'an was revealed."]] This has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent reasoning), and for its permissibility in the presence of the Messenger ﷺ, since they both acted by ijtihad, and by it those who say "every mujtahid is correct" argued.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 59, verse 6–7:

﴿Whatever God restored to His Messenger from them﴾ means: He made it for him alone, a special spoil (fay' khassa). The word al-iyjaf (الإيجاف) derives from al-wujuf (الوجيف), which is rapid travel.

From this is his (ﷺ) saying regarding the departure from Arafat: «Righteousness is not in pressing horses or driving camels (iyda' al-ibil) at speed; keep to your calm (ʿala hinatikum)» [[His words "wa la iyda' al-ibil" — in al-Sihah: "wada'a al-ba'ir wa ghayrahu", meaning he hastened in his pace, and his rider urged it on, i.e., made it hasten in its pace. (ʿA.)]] [[Abu Dawud, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Bazzar and al-Hakim narrated it from the transmission of Miqsam from Ibn ʿAbbas in similar form, and al-Bukhari from another route from Ibn ʿAbbas in part.]]

The meaning of ﴿So you did not press on against it with horse or camel﴾ is: you did not press on, in acquiring and seizing it, with horses or riding camels, nor did you exert yourselves in fighting for it; rather you walked to it on your feet. The meaning is that what God granted His Messenger of the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir is something you did not obtain by fighting and overpowering; rather God gave His Messenger power over them and over what was in their hands, just as He used to give His messengers power over their enemies. Thus the matter concerning it is delegated to him; he places it wherever he wills. That is to say, he does not divide it in the manner of the division of the spoils over which fighting took place and which were taken by force and compulsion. This is because they asked for its division, and so it was revealed.

The conjunction is not attached to this clause, because it explains the first one; it is not foreign to it. It clarifies for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) what he does with what God gave him as fay', and commands him to place it where the khums (one-fifth) of the spoils is placed, divided among the five categories.

As for al-dawla and al-dawla (دولة), with fatha and damma, both have been read; it is what turns in favour of a person, that is, what rotates of good fortune (al-jadd). It is said: "dalat lahu al-dawla" (fortune turned in his favour) and "udila li-fulan" (it was turned to so-and-so). The meaning of His exalted words ﴿so that it does not become a circulation among the rich among you﴾ is: so that the fay', whose right is to be given to the poor so that it becomes for them a sustenance by which they live, does not become a thing circulated among the rich, who multiply through it. Or: so that it does not become a jahili dawla (a circulation of the pre-Islamic kind) among them. The meaning of the jahili dawla is that the chiefs among them used to take the spoils first, because they were the people of leadership, dawla and dominance, and they used to say: "whoever is mighty plunders." The meaning is: so that its seizure is not by dominance and pre-Islamic selfishness. From this is the saying of al-Hasan: "They took the servants of God as servants and the wealth of God as something circulated," meaning: whoever among them overpowered, seized it and monopolised it. It has also been said that "al-dawla" is what is passed around, like al-ghurfa (the scoop), the name of what is scooped; that is, so that the fay' does not become something the rich pass around among themselves and trade, so that it does not reach the poor. And al-dawla with fatha means "circulation," that is: so that it does not become something circulated among them.

Or: so that its retention does not become a circulation among them, without their bringing it out to the poor. It has also been read dawlatun in the nominative, as the complete "kana" (is/exists), like His words ﴿and if there is one in hardship (dhu ʿusra)﴾, meaning: so that there does not occur a jahili circulation, and its effect is cut off; or so that there is no circulation of it among them; or so that there is not some item traded among them that is not brought out to the poor.

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you﴾ of the division of spoil or fay', ﴿take it﴾; and whatever he forbids you from taking of it, ﴿refrain from it﴾ and do not let your souls pursue it. ﴿And fear God﴾ lest you oppose Him, and neglect His commands and prohibitions. ﴿Indeed God is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever opposes His Messenger. The better view is that it is general over everything the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought and forbade, and the matter of fay' falls within its generality.

It is related from Ibn Masʿud (may God be pleased with him) that he met a man in the state of ihram wearing his garments, and said to him: "Take that off you." The man said: "Recite to me a verse of the Book of God concerning this." He said: "Yes," and recited it to him. [[Ibn Abi Shayba narrated it: "Muʿawiya ibn Hisham narrated to us, al-Thawri narrated to us from al-Aʿmash from Ibrahim from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yazid from Ibn Masʿud" with it; and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr in al-ʿIlm narrated it through Yahya ibn Adam from ʿAtiyya and Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbbas from Ibn Ishaq from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd who said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud met..." and mentioned it.]]

As for al-dawla and al-dawla (دولة), with fatha and damma, both have been read; it is what turns in favour of a person, that is, what rotates of good fortune (al-jadd). It is said: "dalat lahu al-dawla" (fortune turned in his favour) and "udila li-fulan" (it was turned to so-and-so). The meaning of His exalted words ﴿so that it does not become a circulation among the rich among you﴾ is: so that the fay', whose right is to be given to the poor so that it becomes for them a sustenance by which they live, does not become a thing circulated among the rich, who multiply through it. Or: so that it does not become a jahili dawla (a circulation of the pre-Islamic kind) among them. The meaning of the jahili dawla is that the chiefs among them used to take the spoils first, because they were the people of leadership, dawla and dominance, and they used to say: "whoever is mighty plunders." The meaning is: so that its seizure is not by dominance and pre-Islamic selfishness. From this is the saying of al-Hasan: "They took the servants of God as servants and the wealth of God as something circulated," meaning: whoever among them overpowered, seized it and monopolised it. It has also been said that "al-dawla" is what is passed around, like al-ghurfa (the scoop), the name of what is scooped; that is, so that the fay' does not become something the rich pass around among themselves and trade, so that it does not reach the poor. And al-dawla with fatha means "circulation," that is: so that it does not become something circulated among them.

Or: so that its retention does not become a circulation among them, without their bringing it out to the poor. It has also been read dawlatun in the nominative, as the complete "kana" (is/exists), like His words ﴿and if there is one in hardship (dhu ʿusra)﴾, meaning: so that there does not occur a jahili circulation, and its effect is cut off; or so that there is no circulation of it among them; or so that there is not some item traded among them that is not brought out to the poor.

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you﴾ of the division of spoil or fay', ﴿take it﴾; and whatever he forbids you from taking of it, ﴿refrain from it﴾ and do not let your souls pursue it. ﴿And fear God﴾ lest you oppose Him, and neglect His commands and prohibitions. ﴿Indeed God is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever opposes His Messenger. The better view is that it is general over everything the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought and forbade, and the matter of fay' falls within its generality.

It is related from Ibn Masʿud (may God be pleased with him) that he met a man in the state of ihram wearing his garments, and said to him: "Take that off you." The man said: "Recite to me a verse of the Book of God concerning this." He said: "Yes," and recited it to him. [[Ibn Abi Shayba narrated it: "Muʿawiya ibn Hisham narrated to us, al-Thawri narrated to us from al-Aʿmash from Ibrahim from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yazid from Ibn Masʿud" with it; and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr in al-ʿIlm narrated it through Yahya ibn Adam from ʿAtiyya and Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbbas from Ibn Ishaq from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd who said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud met..." and mentioned it.]]

[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said:] "It is a substitution (*badal*) for His words *li-dhi al-qurba* ('to the kinsmen') and what follows it." The reason that prevents substituting it for *lillahi wa-li-l-Rasul* ('for Allah and the Messenger') and the words conjoined to them, even though the meaning is 'for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ', is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, removed His Messenger from the poor in His words ﴿and they support Allah and His Messenger﴾. He also raised the Messenger of Allah above being named 'the poor', and substitution according to the apparent wording would contradict what is required in exalting Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Those are the truthful ones﴾ in their faith and their struggle.

[Ahmad said:] The position of Abu Hanifa is that the entitlement of the kinsmen to their shares of the fay' (spoils without fighting) is conditional upon their being poor, so that their wealthy are not entitled to it. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, was harsh in refuting this position, as transmitted from him by Imam al-Haramayn: Allah the Exalted tied entitlement to kinship and did not stipulate need, and disregarding kinship is opposition and defiance. Imam al-Haramayn offered an excuse on behalf of Abu Hanifa: since charity (*sadaqat*) was forbidden to them, the benefit of mentioning them in the fifth of the fay' and the ghanimah (spoils of war) is that the impermissibility of giving them charity does not prevent giving them this share. He then followed this excuse by saying: "It should not be expressed this way, for the wording of the verse explicitly establishes their entitlement, as an honour to them and an alert to the greatness of their rank. Whoever interprets it as permitting giving them the share while countering this permission with the permissibility of depriving them has nullified the implication (*fahwa*) of the verse." The Imam then stressed the gravity of the consequence for them, because they hold that faith must be stipulated in the slave freed for zihar (a form of divorce) beyond what the text states, and they establish this by analogy (*qiyas*), which only yields an inference and is not of the nature of establishing a ruling. He said: "Likewise, it is necessary for them to hold that stipulating poverty in the kinsmen, and stipulating need, is a stipulation that has no basis in the text. As for their own position, which restricts it to the specific descendants of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those rooted in his lineage, like the non-Arabs (*al-ajam*), no justification for their position remains." End of the Imam's words. I quoted him only so it may be known that his objection to Abu Hanifa was based on the fact that Abu Hanifa's stipulation of need rests on analogy or similar external considerations outside the verse. Therefore he held that it adds to the text. But since Abu Hanifa derived the consideration of need from the restriction in the substitution mentioned in the verse, he proceeds with him in a different direction, saying: it is a substitution for the needy and not for anything else.

The explanation is that Allah, glorified is He, wished to describe the needy with attributes that confirm their entitlement and move the wealthy to prefer them, so that they would not find in their hearts any need for what they were given. When He intended this, and had separated their mention from the attributes He intended to describe them by, with His words ﴿so that it does not become a circulating thing among the rich among you﴾ up to ﴿severe in punishment﴾, He refreshed their mention so that it would serve as a preparation for the successive attributes that follow. So He mentioned them with another attribute that corresponds to the first attribute, as a substitution for it, which is poverty, so that the refreshing would attest to the benefit of combining for them the two attributes of destitution and poverty. Then their attributes were recited in succession: their being expelled from their homes and properties as emigrants, their seeking bounty and good pleasure from Allah, their support of Allah and His Messenger, their sincerity in their intentions, and so on to the end. This is what the context guides to, supported by the original principle, for the kinsmen were mentioned with an unrestricted description, so the basic principle is that they remain on that until it is established that they are intended by the restriction. What we have mentioned, directing it to the needy, suffices to uphold the balance of the speech, leaving the kinsmen on the original unrestricted state. This is a principle that the Hanafis cannot repel, for they hold that an exception following a series of sentences applies only to the last sentence, because returning it to the last sentence upholds the balance of the speech and leaves what precedes it on its original footing. There is no difference between an exception and a substitution that follows, and everything other than these. Moreover, if it were made a substitution for the kinsmen together with what follows, its substitution for the kinsmen would be only a partial substitution (*badal al-ba'd min al-kull*), since the kinsmen are divided into poor and wealthy; and its substitution for the needy would be only a substitution of a thing for a thing, when both refer to one and the same entity. Then this substitution would have to be understood in two different senses in one situation, and that is impossible because of the difference and contrast between the two kinds, each of which requires what the other rejects. This much suffices, God willing. On this basis al-Zajjaj parsed the verse, making it a substitution for the needy alone. And Allah, the Exalted, is the One who grants success to what is right.

Wa-alladhina tabawwa'u ("and those who settled") is coordinated with al-muhajirin, and they are the Ansar (the Helpers of Madinah).

If you say: what is the meaning of coupling faith (al-iman) with the abode (al-dar), when one does not say "tabawwa'a al-iman" (settled into faith)? I answer: its meaning is "they settled the abode and sincerely held the faith," like the poet's words:

"I fed her figs and cool water."

Or: they made faith a settled and established home for themselves, because of their firmness in it and their steadfastness upon it, just as they made Madinah such a home.

Or: he meant the abode of hijrah (emigration) and the abode of faith, and so he put the definite article (al-) in "al-dar" in place of the genitive noun, and deleted the noun "dar" from "dar al-iman," placing the genitive in its place.

Or: he named Madinah for being the abode of hijrah and the place where faith appeared, by "al-iman."

Min qablihim: before them, that is, before the muhajirin, because they preceded them in settling the abode of hijrah and faith. It was also said: before their hijrah.

Wa-la yajiduna fi anfusihim hajatan mimma utu: and they do not find in their souls any desire (talab) for what the muhajirin were given of the fay' (spoils) and other things. The one who needs something is called "hajah" (need). It is said: "Take your hajah from him," and "He gave him from his wealth his hajah." The meaning is that their souls did not pursue what was given to others, nor aspired to anything of it that they needed.

Wa-law kana bihim khasasah: even if they had poverty (khallah). Its root is "khasas al-bayt," which are its gaps (furuj). The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: their poverty was assumed.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) divided the wealth of Bani al-Nadir among the muhajirin and gave nothing to the Ansar except three men who were in need: Abu Dujanah Simak ibn Kharashah, Sahl ibn Hunayf, and al-Harith ibn al-Simmah. [Al-Tha'labi mentioned this without a chain. Al-Waqidi narrated from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from Kharijah ibn Zayd, from Umm al-'Ala', who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took the spoils of Bani al-Nadir, he said to Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas: 'Call the Ansar, all of them, for me.'

He said: 'If you wish, I will divide it between you and the muhajirin; and if you wish, I will give them (the wealth) and they will leave your homes.' The two Sa'ds said: 'Rather, let him divide it among the muhajirin, and let them remain in our homes.' The Ansar were content. So he gave to the muhajirin and gave nothing to the Ansar except two needy men, Sahl ibn Hunayf and Abu Dujanah." And Sayf ibn Abi al-Huqayq was attributed to Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, and he had a mention among them. Abu Dawud has part of it from the narration of 'Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar, but he left the names of the two Ansari men unspecified. In Ibn Ishaq's Maghazi: "Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr narrated to me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) divided the wealth of Bani al-Nadir among the first muhajirin, excluding the Ansar, except that Sahl ibn Hunayf and Abu Dujanah mentioned poverty, so he gave to them."]

He said to them: "If you wish, I will divide for the muhajirin from your wealth and your homes, and you will share with them in this spoil; and if you wish, your homes and wealth will remain yours and nothing of the spoil will be divided for you." The Ansar said: "Rather, we will divide for them from our wealth and our homes, and we will prefer them with the spoil and not share in it." So this was revealed.

Al-shuhh (stinginess), with a damma or kasra (both are read): it is baseness (al-lu'm), and that a man's soul be tight and greedy in withholding, as the poet said:

"He struggles with a soul between his ribs, tight-fisted; when he resolves on kindness, it says to him, 'Wait!'"

[He describes a man as stingy, who struggles with the soul between his ribs. Kazzah (with fatha) means stingy and withdrawn from doing good when it overpowers him; when he intends kindness, it calls him back to miserliness and holds him back from giving, as if it said to him, "Wait!" so that he obeys it. Mahlan is a verbal noun whose verb is necessarily deleted. Her saying "dhalika" is a clear metaphor for its whispering of stinginess.]

It is attributed to the soul because it is an innate disposition in it. As for bukhl (miserliness), it is the withholding itself. From it is God's saying: "And souls are present with stinginess" (4:128), and "Whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul" (59:9). Whoever overcomes, by God's help and guidance, what he is commanded and opposes its desire, "those are the successful" (al-muflihun): those who attain what they sought.

It is also read: "wa-man yuqa" (with a different vocalization).

﴿And those who came after them﴾ is also conjoined (ʿaṭf, grammatical coordination) to the emigrants: they are those who emigrated after them.

It was also said: they are the Successors (al-tābiʿūn) who follow them in excellence. Ghill (rancour) is also read as ghamr, and both mean resentment (ḥiqd).

For their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book: between them and them is a brotherhood of disbelief, and because they used to befriend them and treat them as brothers, and they were with them against the believers in secret. ﴿And we will not obey you in regard to anyone, if you are fought against, nor will we obey anyone against you, from the Messenger of Allah and the Muslims, if we are attacked; or in regard to your being forsaken and breaking what we promised you of help﴾ ﴿indeed, they are liars﴾, i.e., in their promises to the Jews. And in this is evidence of the truth of prophethood, because it is a report of unseen matters. If you say: how is it said ﴿and if they help them﴾ after the report that they will not help them? I say: its meaning is: and if they help them on supposition and assumption, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾, and just as He knows what will occur, He knows what would not occur if it did occur, how it would occur.

The meaning: and if the hypocrites help the Jews, the hypocrites will surely be defeated, then they will not be helped afterward; that is, Allah Exalted will destroy them and their hypocrisy will not benefit them, because their disbelief has become manifest. Or: the Jews will surely be defeated, then the help of the hypocrites will not benefit them.

For their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book: between them and them is a brotherhood of disbelief, and because they used to befriend them and treat them as brothers, and they were with them against the believers in secret. ﴿And we will not obey you in regard to anyone, if you are fought against, nor will we obey anyone against you, from the Messenger of Allah and the Muslims, if we are attacked; or in regard to your being forsaken and breaking what we promised you of help﴾ ﴿indeed, they are liars﴾, i.e., in their promises to the Jews. And in this is evidence of the truth of prophethood, because it is a report of unseen matters. If you say: how is it said ﴿and if they help them﴾ after the report that they will not help them? I say: its meaning is: and if they help them on supposition and assumption, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾, and just as He knows what will occur, He knows what would not occur if it did occur, how it would occur.

The meaning: and if the hypocrites help the Jews, the hypocrites will surely be defeated, then they will not be helped afterward; that is, Allah Exalted will destroy them and their hypocrisy will not benefit them, because their disbelief has become manifest. Or: the Jews will surely be defeated, then the help of the hypocrites will not benefit them.

**Verse 13–17**

*Raḥbatan* (رَهْبَةً) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from *rahiba*, used in the passive form (*al-mabnī lil-mafʿūl*, the passive-voice pattern). It is as if it were said: "[You are] more to be feared." His words *fī ṣudūrihim* (in their breasts) indicate their hypocrisy, meaning that they display to you outward fear of God while, in their breasts, you are more awe-inspiring to them than God is. If it is asked: "Were they fearing God, such that their fear of you would be greater?" I answer: the meaning is that their fear of you in secret is greater than their fear of God, which they display to you, though they used to show you intense fear of God. It is also permissible that he means that the Jews fear you in their breasts more than they fear God, because they were a people of might and valour, so they would show courage toward you while concealing dread in their hearts.

*Lā yafqahūna* (they do not comprehend): they do not know God and His greatness, so that they would fear Him with the fear that is due to Him.

*Lā yuqātilūnakum* (they will not fight you): they will not be able to fight you.

*Jamīʿan* (all together): gathered and united, meaning the Jews and the hypocrites.

*Illā kāʾinīna fī quran muḥaṣṣanatin* (except from within fortified towns) by means of trenches and passages, *aw min warāʾi judur* (or from behind walls), without coming out to you (*dūna an yaṣḥarū lakum*) [[Footnote: His words "without coming out to you" — in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "aṣḥara al-rajul" means he went out into the open desert. (ʿ)]] and duelling with you, because God casts terror into their hearts, and because God's support and victory are with you. It is also recited as *judar* with a light pronunciation, and as *jidār* and *judur*, both meaning "wall."

*Baʾsuhum baynahum shadīd* (their violence among themselves is severe): the intense might with which they are described is only among themselves when they fight one another. If they were to fight you, that might and strength would not remain with them, because the brave become cowardly and the mighty become humbled when confronted with the war of God and His Messenger.

*Taḥsabuhum jamīʿan* (you think them united): gathered, in harmony and unity. *Wa qulūbuhum shattā* (but their hearts are divided): scattered, with no harmony between them. That is, there is rancour and enmity among them, so they do not support one another with true support, nor do they shoot from a single bow. This is an encouragement to the believers and a strengthening of their hearts for fighting them. *Qawmun lā yaʿqilūna* (a people who do not reason): the scattering of hearts weakens their strength and helps to undermine them.

*Kamathali alladhīna min qablihim* (like those before them): that is, their likeness is like the likeness of the people of Badr in a recent time. If it is asked: "What is *qarīban* (recently) governed by?" I answer: by *mithl* (likeness), meaning: like the existence of the likeness of the people of Badr recently.

*Dhāqū wabāla amrihim* (they tasted the evil consequence of their affair): the bad outcome of their disbelief and enmity toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ). From their saying *kalaʾun wabīl* (a harsh pasture), meaning: unwholesome, of evil outcome. That is, they tasted the punishment of killing in this world, *wa lahum fī al-ākhirati ʿadhābu al-nār* (and for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire).

The likeness of the hypocrites in inciting the Jews to fight and in promising them victory, then abandoning them and breaking their word, is *kamathali al-shayṭāni idhā istaghwā al-insān* (like the Devil when he misleads man) by his deception, *thumma tabarraʾa minhu fī al-ʿāqibah* (then disowns him in the end). What is meant is his misleading of the Quraysh on the day of Badr, and his saying to them: "No one among the people will overcome you today, and I am your protector," up to his saying: "Indeed, I am free of you" [[Footnote: His words "idhā istaghwā al-insān" — perhaps it is "idh," as in al-Nasafī's wording. (ʿ)]].

Ibn Masʿūd recited *khālidān fīhā* (both abiding therein) as the predicate of *inna* (indeed), and *fī al-nār* (in the Fire) is then a redundant (*laghw*) element. According to the well-known reading, the adverbial phrase is a stable predicate (*mustaqirr*), and *khālidīna fīhā* (abiding therein) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). It is also recited *anā barīʾun* (I am free) and *ʿāqibatahumā* (their outcome) in the nominative.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 59, verse 18–19:

He repeated the command to be mindful of God (taqwa) for emphasis: "And be mindful of God" regarding the performance of obligations, because it is coupled with what is an action; and "be mindful of God" regarding the abandonment of sins, because it is coupled with what runs in the course of a warning. "Tomorrow" (al-ghad) is the Day of Resurrection; He called it by the day that follows your day, bringing it close to you [[Mahmud said: "He called the Day of Resurrection 'tomorrow' to bring it close..." Ahmad said: It has been said regarding God's words "a soul knows what it has presented" (ʿalimat nafsun ma aḥḍarat), like His words "the Day when every soul finds what it has done of good brought forth" (yawma tajidu kullu nafsin ma ʿamilat min khayrin muḥḍaran), until it was said that it is of the reverse of speech in which hyperbole is intended by what is reversed, like His words "Perhaps those who disbelieved would wish..." (rubbama yawaddu alladhina kafaru), so the meaning of "rubba" here is the meaning of "kam" (how many). And more eloquent than it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I leave the horn (of enemies) with fingers yellowed..."

However, al-Zamakhshari fled from this meaning, because what actually occurs is the scarcity of souls that reflect on the matter of the return, so he interpreted it according to a meaning that corresponds to reality. It is possible to observe the matter and it is permissible to take it as meaning the multiplicity of souls commanded to reflect on the return, and that there is no soul except that it has a right to comply with this command. This is a good view, for the verb attributed to "soul" here is not the occurrence of reflection so that it stands alone; rather it is the demand for reflection, which relates generally to every soul. And the fair judgment: what al-Zamakhshari stated is more possible and better, and God is the Granter of success.]] And from al-Hasan: He kept bringing it near until He made it like tomorrow. Similar to it is His words, "as if it had not flourished yesterday" (ka-an lam taghna bil-amsi), meaning: bringing near the past time. And it was said: the Hereafter was expressed as "tomorrow," as if this world and the Hereafter were two days: a day and a tomorrow. If you ask: what is the meaning of indefinite "soul" (nafs) and "tomorrow" (ghad)? I say: as for the indefiniteness of "soul," it is to isolate the souls that look at what is due for the Hereafter, as if He said: let one single soul look into that.

As for the indefiniteness of "tomorrow," it is to magnify it and to leave its matter vague, as if it were said: for a tomorrow whose reality is not known because of its greatness. And from Malik ibn Dinar:

It is written on the gate of Paradise: "We found what we did; we profited what we sent ahead; we lost what we left behind."

"They forgot God" (nasu Allah): they forgot His right, so He made them forgetful of their own selves through abandonment [[Mahmud said: "He made them forgetful through abandonment." Ahmad said: Rather, He created forgetfulness in them.]], so that they did not strive for themselves with what would benefit them with Him. Or: on the Day of Resurrection He shows them the terrors in which they forgot themselves, like His words, "their glance does not return to them" (la yartaddu ilayhim tarfuhum).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 59, verse 23–24:

al-Ghayb (ghayb), that which is non-existent (al-ma'dum), and al-Shahada, that which exists and is perceived, as though one were witnessing it. It has been said: what is hidden from the servants and what they have witnessed. It has been said: the secret and the open. It has been said: this world and the Hereafter.

al-Quddus, with a damma and with a fatha, and it has been read with both: the one who is most exalted in purity (al-nazaha) from what is deemed repugnant. Its counterpart is al-Subbuh (subbuh). In the glorification of the angels: "Subbuh, Quddus, Lord of the angels and the Spirit."

al-Salam is in the sense of safety (al-salama). From it come "Dar al-Salam" and "Salamun 'alaykum." It is described by it as an intensive expression of his being free from every deficiency. Or, in the sense of his granting safety, and al-Mu'min is the giver of security.

It has been read with a fatha on the mim, meaning "the one who is believed in," with the preposition elided, as you say of the people of Musa in the words of God, Most High: "Musa chose from his people" (wa-ikhtara Musa qawmahu), meaning "the chosen ones," in the form of the adjective of the seventy.

al-Muhaymin: the watchful guardian over everything, the one who preserves it. It is of the pattern mufay'il, from amn (security), except that its hamza has been changed into a ha'.

al-Jabbar: the one who overpowers, who compelled his creation to what he willed, i.e., forced them (ajbarahum).

al-Mutakabbir: the one most intensely possessed of greatness and majesty. It has also been said: the one who is exalted above wronging his servants.

al-Khaliq: the one who determines what he brings into existence. al-Bari': the one who distinguishes some of it from other parts by its various forms. al-Musawwir: the one who gives shape.

It is reported from Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a that he read: "al-Bari' al-Musawwir," with a fatha on the waw and a nasb on the ra', meaning: the one who makes free (yabra'u) the one who shapes, i.e., who distinguishes what he forms by variations of configuration.

Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa-ma fi al-ard" (and what is on the earth).

From Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him: I asked my beloved (ﷺ) about the Greatest Name of Allah, and he said:

"Upon you is the end of Surat al-Hashr; recite it often." [Narrated by al-Tha'labi from the narration of 'Ali ibn Ruzayq from Hisham ibn Sa'd from Zayd ibn Aslam from 'Ata' ibn Yasar from him.

And in al-Wahidi, from a hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, raised (to the Prophet): "The Greatest Name of Allah is in six verses at the end of Surat al-Hashr."] So I repeated it to him, and he repeated it to me; I repeated it to him, and he repeated it to me.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Hashr, Allah will forgive him what has preceded of his sins and what has followed." [Narrated by al-Tha'labi from the narration of Yazid ibn Aban from Anas with this wording.]
